seo.title: Karmic tail 21 10 16 compatibility: World, Wheel and Tower
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 10 16 compatibility: The World at the entry, The Wheel of Fortune in the middle, The Tower as the main task, read through Antony and Cleopatra.

title: Karmic tail 21-10-16 in compatibility: when a whole world is not enough for two
short: The couple's karmic tail 21-10-16 begins with The World, the fullest card in the deck, and runs into The Tower. Why does a union that enters its task with the words "we have everything" learn its lesson through a collapse? The answer is written into three roles. The World at the entry to the task is the shared wish to be a whole world to each other, without measure or limits. The Wheel of Fortune in the middle is a path in circles: rise, quarrel, reconciliation and rise again. The Tower as the main task is the day the invented image of the partner falls apart; what the couple has to learn is to meet that day together, not each inside a fortress of their own.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: "new heaven, new earth"
paragraphs: The play opens with two people measuring their love. Their very first exchange (Shakespeare is quoted in the original throughout, Plutarch in Bernadotte Perrin's translation):
— If it be love indeed, tell me how much. — There's beggary in the love that can be reckon'd. — I'll set a bourn how far to be beloved. — Then must thou needs find out new heaven, new earth.

The last line is almost word for word the Book of Revelation: "And I saw a new heaven and a new earth" (21:1), where the old world passes away and a new one opens. The chapter number matches the card's number by chance; the meaning does not. The World at the entry to the task is exactly that promise of a new heaven and a new earth: two people begin by declaring their love bigger than everything else.

In Lisovskaya's reading, point M is what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, a "common language". For a 21-10-16 couple that language is the language of the whole. Antony speaks it in the same scene: "Let Rome in Tiber melt, and the wide arch / Of the ranged empire fall! Here is my space. / Kingdoms are clay." And, embracing Cleopatra, he binds "the world to weet / We stand up peerless". Two people become the measure for the whole world.

Plutarch shows how this language sounds in everyday life. At night Antony, dressed as a servant, roamed Alexandria, stopping at the doors and windows of ordinary people to mock them, and Cleopatra went with him, "wearing the garb of a serving maiden". Once he was fishing, the fish would not bite, and he ordered divers to fasten fish already caught to his hook in secret. Cleopatra saw through the trick, invited her friends to watch the next day, and had one of her own people fasten a salted Pontic herring to his hook. Amid the laughter she said: "Imperator, hand over thy fishing-rod to the fishermen of Pharos and Canopus; thy sport is the hunting of cities, realms, and continents" (Plutarch, Life of Antony, 29). That is The World at the entry: the partners set each other's scale. A joke, an adventure, a dare, and every one of them the size of a world map.

In its plus, such a couple can be seen from far away. The two live unlike everyone else: they move, travel, build a philosophy of life of their own, and many people see them as an ideal couple. But M stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. In the very first scene a messenger brings news from Rome, and Antony answers: "Grates me: the sum." Everything beyond the two of them is noise. Later, handing out kingdoms to his children, Antony gave his son Armenia, Media and Parthia, Parthia, as Plutarch notes, "when he should have subdued it" (54). It was never subdued. The World at the entry easily becomes a world on credit: the couple has already arranged the furniture in a house not yet bought and shared out a future that does not yet exist.

Hence the first clue. A love that has declared itself a whole world cannot make room for a crack. In an ordinary couple a failure is a failure. In a couple with The World at the entry any crack looks like the end of the world, because no spare world was ever planned.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: Cleopatra's twenty deaths
paragraphs: How do you keep a whole world alive if it cannot stand still? You spin it. Cleopatra sends a servant to Antony with precise orders: "See where he is, who's with him, what he does: / I did not send you: if you find him sad, / Say I am dancing; if in mirth, report / That I am sudden sick."

Her attendant Charmian advises the opposite: "In each thing give him way, cross him nothing." Cleopatra answers: "Thou teachest like a fool; the way to lose him." And Antony's Roman friend Enobarbus remarks drily that Cleopatra, at the least noise of bad news, "dies instantly; I have seen her die twenty times upon far poorer moment".

This is The Wheel of Fortune in the middle of the task: for such a couple the path from the wish at M to the task at D runs in circles. And in Shakespeare the wheel works. Enobarbus explains why Antony will never leave Cleopatra: "Age cannot wither her, nor custom stale / Her infinite variety." Other women cloy the appetites they feed, "but she makes hungry / Where most she satisfies". Antony goes to Rome, marries Caesar's sister there ("And though I make this marriage for my peace, / I' the east my pleasure lies") and comes back. Rome, Egypt, Rome again, Egypt again.

Lisovskaya calls the ten a symbol of cycles: rises and crises in a couple follow one another, and the change itself has to be accepted, not fought. In its minus it is a swing of "calm, then conflict", and the feeling that being together is hard and yet something holds. This couple's wheel shows in small things. After a quarrel, a week of model tenderness. Then a chill with no explanation. Then a trip that mends everything. Friends know the cycle by heart and no longer ask what has happened this time.

Plutarch left the most vivid scene of such a wheel, and it is set in a kitchen. A young man studying in Alexandria at the time was shown round by the royal cooks and saw "eight wild boars a-roasting". He assumed a crowd of guests was expected. The cook laughed: there were only about twelve guests, but Antony might ask for supper at once, or put it off and get caught up in conversation, so "not one, but many suppers are arranged; for the precise time is hard to hit" (28). The home of a couple with The Wheel in the middle keeps eight boars at different stages of readiness: in case of tenderness, in case of a quarrel, in case of a sudden departure.

The numbers say the same. The middle of the couple's tail is the sum of the two personal middles, and for couples with this tail it always comes to 37. That is more than 22: the sum overflows and is reduced, 3 + 7 = 10. This couple's Wheel is always born of excess. The play's first line is about excess too: the Roman Philo complains that his general's dotage "o'erflows the measure".

Charmian names the danger of the Wheel in the same scene: "In time we hate that which we often fear." Among the tasks of the ten, Lisovskaya also lists moving away from manipulation, grudges and hysterics. A wheel turned by hand teaches the partner to fear the next turn. And a scene rehearsed twenty times will one day be played at the moment when the game is already over.

sections.h2: Main task: The Tower that struck more than once
paragraphs: The main point of the tail is D, and it is read mostly through the minus: what the couple fails at and what it has to learn. Lisovskaya's first task of The Tower is the collapse of the invented image of the partner, when the person turns out to be someone else entirely. Next to it she sets a second, very recognisable one: when something bad happens, the two look and walk in different directions. The play tests the couple on both tasks twice.

The first time is at Actium. In the thick of the sea battle Cleopatra's sixty ships turn and flee, and Antony, in the words of one of his officers, "like a doting mallard", leaves the fight and flies after her. Plutarch describes what happened on board afterwards. Antony did not look at her: he sat down at the prow holding his head in both hands, and "he spent three days by himself at the prow, either because he was angry with Cleopatra, or ashamed to see her" (67). Only at Taenarum "the women in Cleopatra's company at first brought them into a parley, and then persuaded them to eat and sleep together".

Shakespeare compresses those three days into one scene. Antony: "O, whither hast thou led me, Egypt?" Cleopatra: "Forgive my fearful sails! I little thought / You would have follow'd." Antony: "My heart was to thy rudder tied by the strings." The reproach is spoken, the fault admitted, and then comes a decision, the main task lived in its plus:
Fall not a tear, I say; one of them rates All that is won and lost: give me a kiss; Even this repays me.

"All that is won and lost" is the Wheel's ledger, its gains and losses. A partner's tear is not part of that ledger: it is worth more than the whole account. Antony ends the scene by defying fortune: "Fortune knows / We scorn her most when most she offers blows." The collapse has been lived through together.

The second time is at Alexandria. Before Antony's eyes his fleet raises its oars, salutes Caesar's ships and goes over to the enemy. Antony cries: "All is lost; / This foul Egyptian hath betrayed me." Cleopatra, "fearing his anger and his madness", as Plutarch puts it, shuts herself in her tomb near the temple of Isis, a monument "built surpassingly lofty and beautiful" (74), and has the drop-doors let fall. Then she chooses the Wheel's old move, one more death:
Mardian, go tell him I have slain myself; Say, that the last I spoke was "Antony," And word it, prithee, piteously: hence, Mardian, And bring me how he takes my death.

"Bring me how he takes my death" is a test, a game played with feelings at the moment when the game is already over. Antony believes it. A little later another messenger arrives with the truth and says: "I dread, too late."

What makes the second scene different from the first? After Actium the two, even if on the third day and with someone else's help, talk to each other face to face. At Alexandria they do not speak once until it is too late: between them go messengers, a false report and a test. Each is in a tower of their own. Hers is the tomb with its bolts. He had built his even earlier: after Actium he settled on a mole at Pharos, named the dwelling the Timoneum after the Athenian misanthrope, and, Plutarch says, "hated and distrusted all mankind" (69, 71). That is this couple's Tower in its minus: not the lightning as such, but two fortresses where two people wait out the lightning alone.

Shakespeare's ending is literal. The dying Antony is hoisted on ropes to the window of the monument, and Cleopatra, with her two women, pulls him up with her own hands: "How heavy weighs my lord!" They are together again, at the top of the tower, where nothing can be changed any more. This is tragedy, and Shakespeare plays the minus out to the end. The matrix does not predict endings. It shows a mechanism, and the play contains the way out of it too: the scene after Actium.

One note for real life. Cleopatra's pretended death is a stage device. If someone in a real couple threatens to harm themselves, even "as a test", this is no longer a conversation about cards but a reason to call a local emergency number or a crisis line.

sections.h2: "A tower'd citadel" in the clouds: what really collapses
paragraphs: Before he believes the false report, Antony speaks the strangest speech in the play, a speech about clouds: "Sometimes we see a cloud that's dragonish; / A vapour sometime like a bear or lion, / A tower'd citadel, a pendent rock… / That which is now a horse, even with a thought / The rack dislimns, and makes it indistinct, / As water is in water."

Among the clouds stands "a tower'd citadel", a fortress with towers. Shakespeare's tower is literally made of cloud, and what falls apart is what was only an image. Then Antony speaks about himself: "here I am Antony: / Yet cannot hold this visible shape." This is the play's central discovery about the tail 21-10-16. Lisovskaya writes that the task of The Tower is the collapse of the invented image of the partner. Shakespeare adds that one's own image collapses along with the partner's, because it was built around the other person. Cleopatra was the one "whose bosom was my crownet, my chief end".

What words does Antony find for the betrayal? The language of cards: "she, Eros, has / Pack'd cards with Caesar, and false-play'd my glory / Unto an enemy's triumph." In plain terms, she has stacked the deck with Caesar and played away his glory into an enemy's triumph. In Shakespeare's day triumph was also the name of a card game with trumps, and the English word trump is traced back to triumph. In fifteenth-century Italy the cards that later became the Major Arcana of the tarot were called trionfi, "triumphs". Antony describes his Tower as a hand of cards in which his partner gave the trump to the enemy.

A few minutes later he refutes himself with the same word. Dying, he says: "Not Caesar's valour hath o'erthrown Antony, / But Antony's hath triumph'd on itself." The trump that beat him was in his own hand. And was there a betrayal at all? The play never proves it. Cleopatra's messenger says Antony suspected her of dealing with Caesar, "which never shall be found". The image fell before the facts were known.

In the last act Cleopatra does the opposite. Antony is gone, and she rebuilds his image to the size of the universe: "I dream'd there was an Emperor Antony… / His legs bestrid the ocean: his rear'd arm / Crested the world." Then she asks the Roman Dolabella whether such a man could ever have existed. "Gentle madam, no," he answers. The task of a 21-10-16 couple is to do this in the reverse order: to let go of the invented image while the living person is still beside them.

sections.h2: The Hierophant in the centre: a third voice in the couple
paragraphs: Every couple with the tail 21-10-16 has 5, The Hierophant, in the centre. One hundred per cent, no exceptions. For Lisovskaya the couple's centre is the shared atmosphere between the partners, what lies inside and is not on show. The couple enters its task speaking a language "without measure", yet inside it lives the card of measure: rules, traditions, marriage as an institution, the voice of "how things should be".

In the play that voice is Rome. It is there from the first scene: messengers, letters, an Antony suddenly lost in thought. "He was disposed to mirth; but on the sudden / A Roman thought hath struck him," Cleopatra observes. Rome also arrives as a marriage of alliance: Antony marries Octavia to seal his peace with Caesar, and Enobarbus predicts that "the band that seems to tie their friendship together will be the very strangler of their amity", and that "that which is the strength of their amity shall prove the immediate author of their variance". About Octavia he says three words that read like a portrait of the fifth card: "holy, cold, and still". In Waite's divinatory list for The Hierophant stand exactly "Marriage, alliance, captivity, servitude".

But The Hierophant lives inside the passion itself as well. Enobarbus says of Cleopatra that "vilest things / Become themselves in her: that the holy priests / Bless her when she is riggish". The holy priests bless her even in her wantonness. And in Plutarch the couple founds an institution of its own: "they had an association called The Inimitable Livers, and every day they feasted one another" (28). Two people who have abolished other people's rules at once create their own, with a name and rites. The Alexandrians, Plutarch writes, said that Antony "used the tragic mask with the Romans, but the comic mask with them".

In the lovers' first exchange the centre and the entry are already arguing. "Tell me how much", "I'll set a bourn how far to be beloved": this is The Hierophant's question, a request for measure and form. "Then must thou needs find out new heaven, new earth" is The World's answer. In a living couple this argument is not divided by gender and often changes sides: today one partner asks "let's settle at least something", tomorrow the other.

The Hierophant in the centre is not a third person between the partners but a third voice. In its plus this is a couple where the partners are also friends: they always have something to talk about, and if someone in the house has the last word, it is because both decided so. Lisovskaya advises such couples to create holidays and places of their own. In its minus the same voice turns into a teacher: "it's all wrong", "I know better". The scene is familiar: two people who meant to live unlike everyone else quarrel over whose parents to spend New Year with and who, by the rules, should call first after a fight.

Plutarch also shows the darkest turn such a rite can take. After Actium Antony and Cleopatra "dissolved their famous society of Inimitable Livers, and founded another, not at all inferior to that in daintiness and extravagant outlay, which they called the society of Partners in Death" (71). The same feasts, the same guests; only the name changed. This is how the Wheel turns a couple's own ritual: the form stays, the meaning changes sign. "Us against everyone" quietly becomes "we are doomed". The easiest place to notice it is in the words a couple uses to name itself.

sections.h2: A world made of a chain and a choice: where the three numbers come from
paragraphs: Each point of the couple's matrix is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices. Running through all dates shows that the tail 21-10-16 forms in only two ways. In 96% of such couples one partner has the personal tail 15-20-5 and the other 6-17-11. Then The World at the entry is 15 + 6, The Devil and The Lovers. The Wheel in the middle is 20 + 17 = 37, Judgement and The Star. The Tower as the main task is 5 + 11, The Hierophant and Strength. In the remaining 4% the partners' tails are 12-19-7 and 9-18-9: The World is 12 + 9, The Hanged Man and The Hermit; The Wheel is 19 + 18, The Sun and The Moon; The Tower is 7 + 9, The Chariot and The Hermit. Personal tails have meanings of their own, and those meanings are not carried over here. Here they are only the material from which the couple's cards are built.

Now the second clue. In "The couple's values", the sphere that reads the shared path and what the two are together for, such couples have only two cards: The Devil in 53.6% and The Lovers in 46.4%. Exactly the two from which The World at the entry is assembled in 96% of couples. This couple's whole world is glued together from attachment and choice, and the couple's values show which of the two halves leads.

In Antony both halves sound in a single scene. After hearing the messengers from Rome he says: "These strong Egyptian fetters I must break, / Or lose myself in dotage." That is The Devil's chain, fetters that hold against one's will. But he will not break them; again and again he will choose Egypt, and that is already the choice of The Lovers. Waite's list for The Lovers, incidentally, includes "trials overcome". Lisovskaya names the main lesson of the fifteenth energy as this: nobody belongs to anybody. For a 21-10-16 couple it is the question after every turn of the Wheel: do the two stay together because the fetters will not let go, or because they have chosen each other again?

The rare variant has a detail of its own. There The Wheel is built from The Sun and The Moon, day and night taking turns. In the last act Cleopatra describes Antony's face as the sky: "His face was as the heavens; and therein stuck / A sun and moon, which kept their course, and lighted / The little O, the earth." A sun and a moon keeping their course above a little circle: that is the Wheel.

sections.h2: Waite and Wen: deception is written into The Tower
paragraphs: Waite gives The Tower this divinatory list: "Misery, distress, indigence, adversity, calamity, disgrace, deception, ruin," and adds: "It is a card in particular of unforeseen catastrophe." The last three words come in the same order as the events of the play. Disgrace is Actium, after which Antony says: "I have offended reputation." Deception is the false report of death. Ruin is the ending. The play walks through this list in order three hundred years before Waite's book.

Benebell Wen says two things about the reversed Tower that meet in a single scene. The blow comes because the Seeker "relied on false impressions made by others", and the card may also mean that the Seeker "has been falsely accused of something". At Alexandria both happen at once: Antony falsely accuses Cleopatra of betrayal, and she creates in him the false impression of her death. In its minus, the collapse of a 21-10-16 couple is rarely pure lightning from the sky. More often it involves an untruth told out of fear and an accusation made before the facts.

Waite has a thought about The World that explains this couple's entry. He writes that the card "is perhaps more especially a story of the past, referring to that day when all was declared to be good, when the morning stars sang together". A couple with The World at the entry will recognise this: their common language often sounds like a memory of the beginning, of that trip, of that summer. Among the things that fill a couple with this energy, Lisovskaya names returning to places with good memories. But a story of the past has a reverse side, a demand: "be again who you were then". The dying Antony asks Cleopatra to please her thoughts by "feeding them with those my former fortunes / Wherein I lived, the greatest prince o' the world".
For the reversed Wheel Waite writes not "bad luck", as popular retellings have it, but "Increase, abundance, superfluity": the very eight boars in the Alexandrian kitchen.

On Waite's card the figure of The World dances inside an oval wreath, which he himself calls a garland, "an elliptic garland". When Antony dies, Cleopatra says: "The crown o' the earth doth melt. My lord! / O, wither'd is the garland of the war." The same garland has withered. The World with which the couple entered its task withers at the end of its Tower. The play is a tragedy precisely because Antony and Cleopatra did not play the scene after Actium a second time.

sections.h2: How to get through The Tower together
paragraphs: The main task of the tail does not promise a catastrophe. It says where the couple learns. The play also gives the opposite recipe, the one that worked after Actium.

ul: **Speak face to face, not through messengers.** Antony and Cleopatra's second Tower is played out entirely through go-betweens. The first was survived when the two finally spoke for themselves, even if on the third day.

**Do not turn the Wheel by hand.** "If you find him sad, say I am dancing" works while it is a game. Disappearing "so they miss me", threats to leave and tests of "how will they take it" turn into a false report on the day of a real collapse.

**Separate the event from the verdict on the person.** "The fleet went over to Caesar" is a fact. "She betrayed me" is a conclusion reached in a minute. In the first hours after a blow it is better not to decide who the partner "really" turned out to be.
**Do not keep a ledger of gains and losses.** "Fall not a tear, I say; one of them rates / All that is won and lost": this line takes the couple off the Wheel.

**Call in a third person who brings together rather than judges.** After Actium the couple was reconciled by the women of Cleopatra's household. In life this is a friend both partners trust, or a couples counsellor.

**Remember that what is said in a collapse stays.** In her reading of a couple with The Tower in the centre, Lisovskaya notes that words spoken in a quarrel stay in the memory forever. "Triple-turn'd whore!" is never taken back in any scene.

paragraphs: And the last point, the most unexpected one. The answer to the riddle of this tail lies in the play's very first scene. Cleopatra asked love for a boundary; Antony refused it any measure. A world without measure cannot survive a crack, and every failure becomes the end of the world. **This couple's world needs a measure**, the very one The Hierophant holds in the centre. Then another turn of the Wheel stays a turn, and The Tower becomes the rebuilding of a house rather than the death of a universe.

sections.h2: How to calculate the couple's karmic tail 21-10-16
paragraphs: A couple's tail is not calculated from a single date. Each point of the couple's matrix is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22: if the sum is greater than 22, its digits are added together. The middle of the couple's tail is also added up from the partners' middles, not recalculated from the couple's two outer numbers.
An example: the dates 17.01.1976 and 05.11.1975. The first partner's personal tail is 15-20-5, the second's is 6-17-11. Adding point by point:
In the centre of this couple's chart stands 5, The Hierophant, as in every couple with this tail. In "The couple's values" stands 6, The Lovers.

The tail 21-10-16 occurs in roughly one couple in 107 (0.931%) and ranks 39th of the 97 couple tails. No other couple tails are made of these three numbers: neither 16-10-21 nor any other order forms in a couple. The same order 21-10-16 also occurs as a personal tail, but that is a different calculation with different roles for the points.

intro: Shakespeare put such a couple on stage around 1606. Antony and Cleopatra is a play about two people for whom the whole Roman world is too small, about a love kept alive by constant change, and about a collapse after which each of them locks themselves in a tower. Shakespeare took the story from Plutarch, at times almost word for word. Both of them share a detail that makes this story worth reading for a couple with this tail: Antony and Cleopatra go through a collapse more than once. They come out of the first one together and out of the last one apart. The difference between those scenes is the main task of the tail 21-10-16.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 21-10-16 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of the couple's matrix: The World at the entry to the task, The Wheel of Fortune in the middle, The Tower as the main task. The couple enters its shared task wanting to be a whole world to each other, lives through circles of rises, quarrels and reconciliations, and learns the main thing: to live through the collapse of the invented image of the partner together, not each in a fortress of their own.

faq.q: Is The Tower as the main task a verdict on the couple?
faq.a: No. The main task is read through difficulties, but it does not predict events or dates. The Tower shows where the couple learns: how it meets a blow and what it does with the image of the partner when that image no longer matches the living person. In Shakespeare's play the couple gets through its Tower together at least once, after Actium.

faq.q: How is the couple's tail 21-10-16 different from the personal tail 21-10-16?
faq.a: A personal tail is calculated from one date of birth, and its points mean something else. A couple's tail is the sum of the points of two personal matrices: here 21 is the couple's shared wish, 10 its path, 16 the main task of the union. With this couple tail, the partners' own personal tails are most often 15-20-5 and 6-17-11, not 21-10-16.

faq.q: Can a couple have the tail 16-10-21 or another order of these numbers?
faq.a: No, running through all dates confirms it: only 21-10-16 forms in a couple. The reason is arithmetic. The first number of a couple's tail is always divisible by three, and of these numbers only 21 is. The order 21-16-10 does not work either: the middle of the tail depends on its ends, and between 21 and 10 there can be no 16.

faq.q: Why do such couples always have The Hierophant in the centre?
faq.a: That is how the partners' personal centres add up: with this tail their sum always reduces to 5. The atmosphere inside the couple is The Hierophant: rules and rites of its own and the voice of "how things should be". In its plus this means trust, loyalty and friendship inside the union; in its minus, lecturing and attempts to remake the partner.

faq.q: What should a couple with the tail 21-10-16 do?
faq.a: Talk directly rather than through go-betweens and tests; do not rock the relationship on purpose to keep interest alive; after a blow, separate the fact from the verdict on the partner; do not keep score of gains and losses; call in someone who reconciles rather than judges. And give the shared world a measure: then a crack stays a crack rather than the end of the world.

report: The lovers' first exchange in Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra is an argument about measure. "If it be love indeed, tell me how much," says Cleopatra. "There's beggary in the love that can be reckon'd," Antony answers. "I'll set a bourn how far to be beloved." — "Then must thou needs find out new heaven, new earth." The last line is almost word for word the Book of Revelation. The whole karmic tail 21-10-16 is already written into this exchange: the couple enters its task with The World, travels it on The Wheel of Fortune and learns its lesson from The Tower.

report.h3: A world with no room for a crack

Antony speaks it from the first scene: "Let Rome in Tiber melt… Kingdoms are clay." Plutarch writes that "he spent three days by himself at the prow, either because he was angry with Cleopatra, or ashamed to see her", until the women of her household brought the two into a parley. In Shakespeare the reproach is spoken, the fault admitted, and then comes a decision: "Fall not a tear, I say; one of them rates / All that is won and lost." The collapse is lived through together.

At Alexandria the fleet goes over to Caesar, and Antony cries: "This foul Egyptian hath betrayed me." Cleopatra locks herself in her tomb and sends a messenger to say she has killed herself: "And word it, prithee, piteously: hence, Mardian, / And bring me how he takes my death." The Wheel's old move, a test, is played at the hour of collapse. Antony believes it. The messenger with the truth arrives saying: "I dread, too late."

The difference between the two scenes is the key to the tail. After Actium the two talk face to face; at Alexandria, only through messengers. **Each is in a tower of their own**: she in the tomb with its bolts, he, even earlier, in a dwelling on a mole at Pharos, named after the misanthrope Timon. The play is a tragedy and plays the minus out to the end; the tail predicts no endings, it shows a mechanism. If someone in a real couple threatens to harm themselves, even "as a test", that is a reason to call a local emergency number or a crisis line.

report.h3: The trump in his own hand

report: Before he believes the false report, Antony watches the clouds: now a dragon, now a lion, now "a tower'd citadel", and suddenly everything loses its outline, "as water is in water". "Here I am Antony: / Yet cannot hold this visible shape." With the partner's image one's own collapses too, because it was built around the other person: Cleopatra was the one "whose bosom was my crownet, my chief end".

Antony describes the betrayal in the language of cards: she has "pack'd cards with Caesar, and false-play'd my glory / Unto an enemy's triumph". Triumph was a game with trumps, and the word trump comes from it; in fifteenth-century Italy "triumphs" were the cards that later became the Major Arcana. Dying, Antony says: "Not Caesar's valour hath o'erthrown Antony, / But Antony's hath triumph'd on itself." **The trump that beat him was in his own hand.** The play never proves the betrayal: the image fell before the facts were known.

Such couples always have The Hierophant in the centre: rules, rites, the voice of "how things should be". It is not a third person but a third voice. In the play it sounds as Rome and as the couple's own rites: they called their circle the Inimitable Livers, and after Actium they dissolved it and founded a new one, the Partners in Death. The same feasts, a different name: this is how the Wheel changes the sign of a ritual, and "us against everyone" quietly becomes "we are doomed".
The play itself suggests the way out:

ul: speak face to face, not through messengers and tests;
do not turn the Wheel by hand: disappearing "so they miss me" and threats to leave turn into a false report during a real collapse;
separate the event from the verdict on the person: "the fleet went over to Caesar" is a fact, "she betrayed me" is a conclusion reached in a minute;
call in a third person who brings together rather than judges, a friend or a couples counsellor.

report: The answer to the riddle of the tail lies in the first scene. Cleopatra asked love for a boundary; Antony refused it any measure. **This couple's world needs a measure**, the one The Hierophant holds in the centre. Then a turn of the Wheel stays a turn, and The Tower becomes the rebuilding of a house rather than the death of a universe.
